Q: Print capture groups for every match A:

Replace for with while:

... | perl -Mv5.14 -wne'say "$1-->$2" while /(\d)([a-z])/g'

With the for loop, the regex is computed in a list context, causing very different behavior.

In particular, this is about the behavior of /g modifier in list-vs-scalar context. From perlop:

The /g modifier specifies global pattern matching--that is, matching as many times as possible within the string. How it behaves depends on the context. In list context, it returns a list of the substrings matched by any capturing parentheses in the regular expression. If there are no parentheses, it returns a list of all the matched strings, as if there were parentheses around the whole pattern.

In scalar context, each execution of m//g finds the next match, returning true if it matches, and false if there is no further match. The position after the last match can be read or set using the pos() function; see "pos" in perlfunc. A failed match normally resets the search position to the beginning of the string, but you can avoid that by adding the /c modifier (for example, m//gc). Modifying the target string also resets the search position.

In the for loop's list the regex is in list context and we get back all captures -- with $1 and $2 being set to the last two, so in each for loop iteration we get those same two. But the while loop sets the scalar context for its condition and then /g iterates through matches in the string, so each time we get back the next pair of the specified two captures, with the corresponding $1 and $2.

  • The -Mv5.14 is there for say, as the simple -E isn't good for future. Thanks to ikegami

  • That \d is Unicode and locale-aware, and it matches anything that has \p{Digit} property. That's some 300-odd characters, I think, from various writing systems and this can be very misleading or even dangerous, if you cross paths with Unicode.

    One can constrain it to ASCII by the /a modifier, but why not use [0-9] if you want ASCII?

    See perlrecharclass and for instance this Stack Overflow page. Also, ask AI for examples, like: Perl show examples of what kinds of Unicode characters the \d pattern for a digit matches in a regex

Q: How to fix this integer print routine in real-mode assembly? A:

For some reason this code just won't work.

cmp si, 0
jl .negative

.negative:

This can't work! Jumping-to AND falling-through into .negative will treat every value as negative. The quick fix would be to reverse the conditional and replace jl .negative with jge .loop. But why would you keep your current solution that is rather convoluted?

2nd stage, which has enough space for that code

True, but wasting bytes is never a good idea...

Since you print the result, character by character, there's a better way to solve this, not requiring setting up a buffer (and the hassle to address it). Additionally you can avoid the complexity of maintaining a flag for the minus sign, as we can print the character right away. Displaying numbers with DOS has more info on how to display numbers. The fact that it mentions DOS is of no importance because you can simply exchange DOS with BIOS Teletype, which is exactly what I did here.

Below is my suggestion for a much smaller and clearer version:

; Prints an integer to the screen
; IN (si,di) OUT () MOD (ax,dx)
print_int:
      push si       ; SI is integer number
      cmp  di, 2    ; DI is base [2,36]
      jl   .RET
      cmp  di, 36
      jg   .RET

      cmp  di, 10
      jne  .NUM     ; Always positive for non-base 10
      test si, si
      jns  .NUM
.NEG: neg  si
      mov  ax, 0Eh<<8 + '-'
      int  10h      ; BIOS.Teletype (putc)

.NUM: mov  ax, si
      push di       ; Sentinel
.DIV: xor  dx, dx
      div  di
      push dx       ; Remainder [0,35]
      test ax, ax
      jnz  .DIV

      pop  si       ; First pop is a remainder for sure
.POP: mov  al, [digits + si]
      mov  ah, 0Eh
      int  10h      ; BIOS.Teletype (putc)
      pop  si
      cmp  si, di
      jb   .POP     ; Keep popping until we pop the sentinel
.RET: pop  si
      ret

digits: db "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"

Q: Why my about page in Pelican returns 404? A:

It doesn't look like you set the slug for your page, so it's defaulting to "about-us" from the title. That means the page is being built at /about-us, hence why nothing appears at /about. Try checking localhost:8000/about-us to see if that's the problem, and if so, adding the line Slug: about to your about.html.
